The Iberian Peninsula. The southwestern corner of Europe, containing the modern nations of Spain and Portugal plus a small part of France. Home to multiple civilizations—Lusitanians, Romans, Visigoths, Moors—the peninsula was the stage for centuries of cultural, religious, and military conflict, particularly the Reconquista, the Christian reconquest of territories ruled by Islamic Moorish kingdoms.

The Iberian Peninsula was inhabited by indigenous Lusitanians and Celtiberians before Roman conquest in the second century BCE, becoming the Roman provinces of Lusitania, modern Portugal, and Hispania, modern Spain. Following Rome's collapse, the peninsula was conquered by the Visigoths, a Germanic Christian kingdom, in the early fifth century, establishing kingdoms that ruled until the early eighth century. The Umayyad Caliphate invaded the peninsula in seven hundred eleven CE, rapidly conquering Visigothic kingdoms and establishing Islamic rule in what became known as Al-Andalus, a sophisticated Islamic civilization enduring until the fifteenth century.

Al-Andalus was renowned for cultural and scientific achievement. Cordoba became one of the world's greatest cities with libraries, philosophers, mathematicians, and poets. Toledo was a center of translation and intellectual exchange. The Reconquista, the Christian reconquest, began in the ninth century as Christian kingdoms in the north gradually reconquered territory from Moorish, or North African Islamic, kingdoms, a process lasting nearly eight hundred years. By the thirteenth century, only the kingdom of Granada remained under Islamic rule. The Reconquista culminated in fourteen ninety-two when the Catholic Monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella conquered Granada, ending Islamic rule on the peninsula.

The Alhambra, Granada's magnificent Islamic palace, exemplifies the architectural and artistic sophistication of Islamic Al-Andalus and remains one of the world's great monuments. The blending of Christian and Islamic cultures created distinctive Iberian or Spanish culture. Architecture combined Moorish and Christian elements, language incorporated Arabic words, and literature and philosophy synthesized Christian and Islamic traditions. In fourteen ninety-two, the same year Granada fell, Christopher Columbus sailed for the Americas under the sponsorship of Ferdinand and Isabella, initiating Spanish exploration and colonial empire across the Atlantic.
